# Longitude by lunar distances (`longitude_lunar_distances`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/navigation.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Navigation, transport & exploration (`navigation`)
- Deps: needs reflecting_octant_sextant; helped by latitude_astrolabe_quadrant, logarithms
- Core idea: The Moon moves about its own width (half a degree) per hour against the stars, so it is a clock in the sky: measure its angle to a bright star, look up in a printed almanac at what Greenwich time that angle occurs, and the difference from local time gives longitude (four minutes of time equal one degree). The method needs very accurate lunar tables (Mayer, from Newtonian theory) and about half an hour of calculation, and gives longitude to about half a degree.
- Pitfalls:
  - Proposing lunar distances in 1490: the instruments and the tables, both accurate to about a minute of arc, are more than 250 years away
  - Forgetting to correct for refraction, parallax of the Moon and the height of the eye; uncorrected the result is degrees off
  - Crediting Vespucci or Columbus with real longitudes; Vespucci's 1499 Moon–Mars conjunction and Columbus's eclipse timings (1494, 1504) gave errors of many degrees
- History: europe: 1499 – Vespucci times a Moon–Mars conjunction; 1514 Johannes Werner proposes the lunar-distance method; 1755 Tobias Mayer's lunar tables; 1767 Maskelyne's first Nautical Almanac
- Read:
  - Nevil Maskelyne, The British Mariner's Guide (1763)
  - Derek Howse, Greenwich Time and the Discovery of the Longitude (1980)
